title: SimpleDateFormat is NOT thread-safe: mutable Calendar state, ThreadLocal fix, DateTimeFormatter best
keyPoints: SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe because format() and parse() write to a shared internal Calendar field.
Two threads sharing one SimpleDateFormat instance produce garbled dates, wrong dates, or NumberFormatException.
Fix 1: create a new SimpleDateFormat per call (safe but slow due to object creation overhead).
Fix 2: wrap in ThreadLocal so each thread has its own instance (safe and reusable, but call remove() in pools).
Fix 3: use DateTimeFormatter from java.time (Java 8+), which is immutable and thread-safe by design.
Always prefer java.time (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, DateTimeFormatter) in new code.

s1_definition.oneliner: SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe because it writes to a shared mutable Calendar field internally; fix it with ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> or, better, use the immutable DateTimeFormatter from java.time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **SimpleDateFormat** – not thread-safe because `format()` and `parse()` internally write to a mutable `Calendar` field shared across all calls.
- **Corruption symptoms** – garbled dates, wrong dates, `NumberFormatException`, or `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` when two threads use the same instance.
- **Fix 1: new instance per call** – safe but creates garbage on every call, adding GC pressure at high throughput.
- **Fix 2: ThreadLocal** – one instance per thread, reused within the thread, no sharing, no corruption.
- **Fix 3: DateTimeFormatter** – immutable and thread-safe by design since Java 8; a single `static final` instance shared safely by all threads.
- **Best practice** – always use `java.time` classes (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, DateTimeFormatter) in new code.
s1_definition.analogy: SimpleDateFormat is like a shared calculator on a desk at National Bank of India. Teller-1 types the date "25/10/2024" and the calculator shows an intermediate result. Teller-2 types "15/03/2025" simultaneously on the same calculator, and both results are garbled: "35/13/2025." ThreadLocal gives each teller their own calculator. DateTimeFormatter is a read-only printed conversion chart on the wall: 100 tellers read it simultaneously with no corruption because nobody writes on it.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  SimpleDateFormat (NOT thread-safe)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Internal mutable Calendar field  │
  │                                   │
  │  Thread-1: calendar.setTime(d1)  │
  │  Thread-2: calendar.setTime(d2)  │←── OVERWRITES!
  │  Thread-1: subFormat() reads d2  │←── WRONG DATA!
  └──────────────────────────────────┘

  DateTimeFormatter (thread-safe)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Immutable: no internal state     │
  │                                   │
  │  Thread-1: format(d1) → OK       │
  │  Thread-2: format(d2) → OK       │
  │  No shared state to corrupt       │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
SimpleDateFormat is one of the most common sources of concurrency bugs in Java applications. It holds a mutable Calendar field internally, and format() and parse() write to this field on every call. Two threads sharing one instance corrupt each other's data, producing garbled dates, wrong dates, or NumberFormatException.

Three fixes exist. Creating a new instance per call is safe but adds GC pressure at high throughput. ThreadLocal gives each thread its own instance with no sharing, but you must call remove() in thread pools to avoid memory leaks. DateTimeFormatter from java.time is the best solution: it is immutable and thread-safe by design, so a single static final instance can be shared by all threads with no ThreadLocal, no remove(), and no bugs.

At National Bank of India, a trade confirmation service with 200 threads used a static SimpleDateFormat. It garbled 50 confirmation dates per day for two months before anyone noticed. Replacing it with a static final DateTimeFormatter eliminated the bug completely with zero overhead.

Remember one sentence: SimpleDateFormat is mutable and broken under concurrency; use DateTimeFormatter, which is immutable and safe.
